title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Sao Paulo?
excerpt:
The first race of 2026 without a Mercedes driver on the podium was ironically where the team clinched the Constructors’ Championship, with Lando Norris and the Red Bull pair denying them a spot in the top three in Sao Paulo. But who impressed our Power Rankings judges? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below…

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

With other teams switching their resources to 2027, McLaren were the only ones to bring upgrades to Interlagos, but Norris was cautious of anticipating any major improvement. While it’s difficult to say just how much they helped considering the way the weather jumbled up the pecking order, Norris’ skill in the wet was clear as he converted pole position to his third triumph of the season. One of the main factors that contributed to his 14s winning margin was, in his words, an ability to keep it cool and avoid mistakes.

Was it really a Sao Paulo Grand Prix if Max Verstappen didn’t charge from the back of the field to the podium? After his stellar comeback drives in 2024 and 2025, he pulled off another by climbing from P21 to P5 during his opening stint on the intermediate tyres. The softs weren’t as good to him, but he caught his team mate to improve to second place and simultaneously take a stronger grip of P2 in the drivers’ standings.

Liam Lawson was arguably the biggest winner of the Qualifying chaos at the rain-soaked Interlagos, with his original result of P5 becoming P3 once the final order had shaken out. He made the most of it too, joining Kimi Antonelli in storming past Norris on the opening lap, but was passed by the top teams as the race progressed. Nevertheless, his admirable defence against Charles Leclerc paid off when the latter was handed a five-second time penalty for making contact in their wheel-to-wheel contest, elevating Lawson to P7 post-race.

Although Isack Hadjar hasn’t been satisfied with the handling of his RB22 in recent rounds, he seemed to turn a corner in Sao Paulo as he excelled in the challenging conditions. Starting fifth, he had the opposite experience to Verstappen and performed best on the soft tyres, getting stuck into several thrilling battles with Antonelli en route to finishing on the podium for the first time since the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Interlagos is where Fernando Alonso secured both of his Drivers’ Championships, and two decades later, he still goes well there. The Spaniard delivered Aston Martin’s first Q3 appearance of the season before tackling a tantalising fight with Alex Albon, which saw him pounce when the Williams driver drifted wide. He still lacked that little bit extra to break into the points, bringing home a respectable P12.

Wet weather always opens up opportunities for the midfield, and the Sao Paulo Grand Prix was no exception. A strong Qualifying led to Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg lining up on the second row, but he didn’t get the launch he needed and immediately lost positions. While that left him scrapping with Franco Colapinto at the fringes of the points, a 10-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage appeared to rule the German out of top-10 contention. However, the late rain played into his hands and he overtook Arvid Lindblad for P10.

A power unit issue cut Lindblad’s Qualifying session short and prompted Racing Bulls to replace his internal combustion engine and turbocharger, resulting in another grid penalty. It would’ve been easy to forget that he started from P18 as he quickly surged through the field, challenging the likes of Alonso and Hulkenberg throughout, although he was unable to hold off the Audi man for P10 over the final laps.

Undaunted by his grid penalty, Lewis Hamilton gained an astonishing 11 positions at the start – and for a few laps, it looked as though he could produce a Verstappen-style comeback to challenge for the podium. However, his tyres rapidly faded and he tumbled back down the order, so it was no surprise that he wanted to gamble by being the first to pit for slicks. He enjoyed another boost by doing just that, but his race unravelled when the rain returned, with a spin and late stop limiting him to P9.

Although a five-place grid penalty meant that it was impossible for George Russell to start on pole, he was still furious when the team’s call to abandon his second Q3 lap left him to qualify behind Norris and subsequently drop to P7. He made good progress on the inters before losing any advantage he had when he switched to slicks, as shown by his unusual spin at the pit exit. After that, the pace gradually came back to him and he passed Antonelli for P4 – his best finish since winning in Baku.

“Extremely disappointed,” was Antonelli’s verdict of his performance at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with the Italian much more content to focus on Mercedes’ overall victory as a team. His initial launch saw him snatch the lead from Norris and build a commanding gap, but like Russell, his race unravelled on the soft tyres. A lack of grip caused Antonelli to spin at Turn 1 and let Norris back through, and he lost out further when the rain fell later on, leaving him to settle for P5.

Missing out

Just missing out on this week’s Power Rankings leaderboard are Haas' Ollie Bearman (17th, after contact with Alonso, slow pit stops and a penalty for an unsafe release) and Williams' Albon (15th, after losing pace when the track dried out).

title: F1 ACADEMY announces 2027 calendar
excerpt:
F1 ACADEMY has revealed its calendar for the 2027 campaign, with the all-female series’ fifth season featuring seven rounds.

The series will continue to support Formula 1 across rounds in Asia, Europe and North America next year.

The 2027 campaign will commence at the Jeddah Corniche Circuit in Saudi Arabia in March, before heading to Shanghai in April and Montreal’s Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve a month later.

A European double-header kicks off with a visit to Silverstone on July 2-4. The series then heads to Budapest for the first time, with the Hungaroring becoming the 17th circuit to feature an F1 ACADEMY round on July 30 – August 1.

F1 ACADEMY returns to action with two trips to the United States, racing around the Circuit of The Americas in Austin in late October. The 2027 season will once again draw to a close under the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit in November.

DateVenueMarch 19-21Jeddah Corniche Circuit, Saudi ArabiaApril 16-18Shanghai International Circuit, ChinaMay 21-23Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, CanadaJuly 2-4Silverstone Circuit, Great BritainJuly 30 – August 1Hungaroring, HungaryOctober 22-24Circuit of The Americas, United StatesNovember 18-20Las Vegas Strip Circuit, United States

Susie Wolff, Managing Director of F1 ACADEMY, said: “It’s hard to believe we’re already heading into our fifth season of F1 ACADEMY. What we’ve collectively achieved in such a short space of time is something we can all be proud of, and I’m equally excited about what lies ahead.

“With our 2027 calendar, we’re continuing to build consistency in where we race, which is important for our drivers, teams and fans. I’m hugely grateful to our promoters for their continued support and belief in what we’re building.

“Every season we’re seeing more fans, more young girls inspired to get involved in motorsport and more opportunities for female talent. The level of competition continues to rise year on year, and we’ve seen some incredible racing as a result. I’m excited to see that level pushed even higher in 2027.”

title: Camara experiences every condition in ‘tricky’ Haas debut
excerpt:
While Rafael Camara saw the chequered flag in a “tricky” debut race for Haas last weekend, the Brazilian faced with the tough task of navigating his first Grand Prix on home soil and in changeable conditions.

The F2 star had already been announced as one of Haas’ drivers for next season, but when the team opted not to field Esteban Ocon, Camara was given the opportunity to make his debut ahead of schedule.

He was able to take part in all three practice sessions to try and find his way with the VF-26, but those were completed in the dry – Qualifying was another matter. The heavens opened, the track was red flagged and Camara was faced with some of the most difficult conditions in recent memory.

He hit the barriers in Q1, had the composure to get back to the pits with a broken front wing, and the guts to go back out and stick another lap in – which was good enough for Q2. But then the rookie crashed out at the end of that segment, locking up and going straight into the barriers.

“I was just a bit unlucky in the last corner, locking up, and then trying to make the corner, but it was really not possible," was his mature take on how Saturday had gone.

"In a way, I’m a bit disappointed with the mistakes, as I know for the team, that’s not what they want, but overall I think it was a positive session.”

With rain falling again on Sunday, conditions were not getting any easier for Camara, who started 11th thanks to grid penalties for some ahead. He lost ground off the line and skated wide again, but was able to keep going and finished in 20th place.

“It definitely wasn’t an easy one, with all the conditions out there we experienced over the course of one race. In the beginning, it was about staying on track, and there were a couple of mistakes – it was a bit tricky,” he admitted.

5 Winners and 5 Losers from Sao Paulo

“The positive is that there was no damage today and lots learned, but there’s still a lot more to learn for the future. I think there are a lot of things to go through with the team and put in place for next time.

“On one side, I was trying to enjoy my first race in Formula 1, at home, so it was nice – but I think on my side, I wasn’t fully satisfied with how we finished today. It was a weekend where I think I must’ve nearly experienced everything, so I’ve learned a lot for the future.”

Ollie Bearman in the other Haas car started in the top 10 and came home in 17th after a slow pit stop, so both drivers went backwards in Brazil on a tough day that saw Audi close to within three points of the American outfit in the fight for seventh in the constructors’ battle.

Given the Brazilian finished at Interlagos, experiencing a drying track, the crossover between intermediate and slick tyres and then the pitfalls of slithering back to the pits for more inters as the rain fell, he has ticked a fair few boxes on debut, and impressed people in the paddock.

"I had a look [on Saturday], until the last corner, he did a mega lap at the beginning of the Quali, and this lap would have been a super lap," Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur said of Camara's performance.

"But honestly, to start in F1, when it's your home race, you have these kind of conditions, that you have to put in inter, medium, soft... It's wet during Quali and the same [in the] race, mega cold conditions today, it was probably the most difficult weekend that he could have had, but he's doing very well. The pace was impressive yesterday."

Haas boss Ayao Komatsu agreed: "He made some mistakes, but overall, I think they were very challenging conditions to make your debut, so well done to him for completing this race without any big issues. We know he has performance, he has speed, it’s just about consistency and delivering it."

title: Why McLaren went the opposite way to Mercedes' front wing
excerpt:
Just underscoring the idea that what works for one car won’t necessarily be good for another, McLaren have made precisely the opposite change in their front wing philosophy to that recently made by Mercedes.

The new McLaren wing in Sao Paulo is joined to the nose via the middle of the three elements rather than the bottom element used previously. Mercedes made the opposite change at the recent US Grand Prix.

title: Alonso credits ‘phenomenal’ car after strong drive in Brazil
excerpt:
After a difficult time of it in Mexico City, Aston Martin bounced back strongly in Brazil as Fernando Alonso finished 12th at Interlagos, just missing out on a rare chance to score points.

The Spaniard showed all his experience in the wet on Saturday to qualify inside the top 10 for the first time all season, and managed to remain up the order in the first stint of the race in what he called a “phenomenal” car.

Even after he started to drop backwards, Alonso was able to fight with the cars around him, which included some of the more typical front runners – the Aston Martin man overtaking Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari on merit at one point.

While his drive did not yield any points, it still left Alonso in a buoyant mood post-race.

“I think it was the best race for the car feeling today," he said. "The car was phenomenal in the corners and we were battling with the Ferraris at one point.

“Even the last five laps on the inters, we were in the mix with the two Mercedes, one lap down, but with the Mercedes. Taking into account how much we lose on the straights, that means probably today we could have been maybe one second faster than them per lap. As I said the car was phenomenal.”

While Alonso’s ‘one second faster’ comment seemed tongue in cheek, what was clear was how much quicker the AMR26 was in Brazil than it has been for much of the season.

His drive was also a good response to Mexico City, where the team had to retire both cars early on with power unit problems, and Alonso’s Sao Paulo performance saw him beat both Alpines, both Williams cars and the two Haas drivers to the flag on merit.

5 Winners and 5 Losers from Sao Paulo

Lance Stroll, however, did not make the end of the race – retiring again with an ERS issue for his eighth DNF in the last 10 Grands Prix.

But Chief Trackside Officer Mike Krack was upbeat in the wake of the race, choosing to look at the weekend as a whole.

“Mixed fortunes for us today," he explained. "A strong drive from Fernando to finish P12 and Lance unfortunately retiring with a battery issue.

"Overall we must be satisfied with the outcome of the weekend as we were ahead of competitors with faster cars in Qualifying and race.”

“We always look forward to racing here in Sao Paulo – an iconic track with a passionate crowd - so it was great to deliver a strong performance in front of the Brazilian fans.”

Aston Martin remain 10th in the standings, five points adrift of Williams.

Alonso last scored in Malaysia, but Aston Martin are seemingly heading in the right direction on pace, even if reliablity remains an Achilles' heel.

title: P10 in Sao Paulo GP 'the maximum possible' – Hulkenberg
excerpt:
Nico Hulkenberg believes that P10 and the final point on offer was "the maximum possible" in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, the Audi driver having recovered from a 10-second penalty.

Hulkenberg lined up fourth on the grid for last Sunday's 71-lap race in Brazil, the German having starred in a wet Qualifying session and promoted two spots by grid penalties for George Russell and Charles Leclerc.

The Audi racer eventually slipped down the order in the Grand Prix as wet conditions at the start soon dried, and found himself battling Franco Colapinto's Alpine on fringes of the points.

Hulkenberg moved ahead at Turn 1 but only after cutting the track, meaning he received a 10-second penalty, which the German served at a late pit stop as drivers pitted for intermediate tyres amid another rain shower.

Having dropped to P11, Hulkenberg charged after Arvid Lindblad before passing the Racing Bulls driver seven laps from the end.

"It was a good move [on Lindblad], set him up a little bit on the entry for the exit with an undercut. It felt nice, felt good, especially after the penalty, obviously to fight back for that position," said Hulkenberg.

"I think that was the maximum possible really today. We didn't have that much pace to offer on the slick or the intermediates, so we'll have to take that and review."

The result was only Hulkenberg's fifth time in the points during a Grand Prix this season, with Audi reducing the gap to Haas for P7 in the teams' standings down to just three points.

Team mate Gabriel Bortoleto finished P16, the Brazilian home hero having crashed out early in Qualifying, which ultimately left him P19 on the grid.

"When I was able to be in free air and put some pace out there [it] was very positive," he said.

"But obviously it's a consequence of yesterday, starting from the back you need to overtake people. Was not easy to overtake because obviously we are limited by the power that we have when it's raining, so we're limited to 250Kw.

"Difficult to get some top speed difference on the straight and I got a bit stuck behind other cars, and when I managed to get free air the pace was very positive and also in the wet at the end, when we put on the inter was very good.

"It's a shame, I think home race was not how I expected. The love from the fans was there and I really appreciate it, so we go to the next one."

title: Kimi Antonelli handed verdict over future Ferrari drive: 'He could go tomorrow'
excerpt:
Guenther Steiner has no doubt Kimi Antonelli will one day drive for Ferrari.

Incoming F1 champion Antonelli is contracted to the Brackley-based squad until at least the end of 2027 after the team exercised an option on his deal. Despite enjoying a flying start to the season, though, Mercedes' dominance has slipped of late.

Naturally, given Antonelli's Italian heritage, and the fact Ferrari is approaching two decades since its last drivers' champion, there has been speculation over a longer-term move to Ferrari.

Former Haas team principal Steiner sees it as a matter of when, rather than if, the 20-year-old will one day drive for the Scuderia.

Asked whether he could envisage Antonelli at Ferrari, speaking to RacingNews365, Italian Steiner replied: "Some people ask why he is not driving for us. That's the only not-so-perfect thing for Italy, that there is an Italian champion not driving for Ferrari.

"But I think at some stage. Think about it. He's 20 years old. He's so young, so at some stage, in my opinion, he will drive for Ferrari.

"Will it be short term? No. It will be maybe 10 years out. But at some stage, obviously, as an Italian with this talent, he will get there.

"I would turn it around. They will get him. He could go tomorrow if he wants."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli in 'right place at right time'

Steiner, who has expressed pride in Antonelli's achieve, has also suggested his ascension this year could mark the beginning of a dominant period for the youngster, pointing to the timing of his arrival alongside F1's new technical rules.

Asked if this could be the start of an era for the Italian, Steiner said: "Yes. He's there the first year of these new regulations.

"In motorsport, especially F1, you need to be at the right place at the right time, and he's hit that - he's at the right place at the right time.

"But Mercedes, with these regulations, are very strong. They are not dominating, which is good for everybody.

"It means he cannot be told 'Just win, because you have got the best machine'.

"No, he wins because he's got a good machine and he's the best at the moment, but I'm pretty sure he will win a few more world championships."

title: FIA called to intervene after Lando Norris injury near-miss:  ‘He’s very lucky’
excerpt:
David Coulthard has called on the FIA to review its podium safety procedures after Lando Norris once again smashed a champagne bottle against the floor during his São Paulo Grand Prix celebrations, warning that the McLaren driver was "very lucky" to escape injury.

Norris sealed a dominant win at Interlagos, surviving changeable conditions that forced multiple tyre switches across the 71-lap race.

But his post-race celebrations once again saw him slam a bottle hard enough to shatter it, echoing a similar incident at Monza in 2020 that left him with cuts to his hand.

The 2025 world champion's podium trouble was not solely smashing his champagne bottle, as he followed it up by accidentally putting his face into the pyrotechnic sparks.

Coulthard, speaking on the Up to Speed podcast, said the Briton needs to break the habit before it causes serious harm.

"I was really impressed across the board, with some standout performances," Coulthard said. "The obvious one is Lando, absolutely brilliant. Although we have to address right at the top that he's got to stop doing the same thing and expecting a different outcome.

"Banging the bottle, like right here, kids, banging glass on anything is not a good idea. You teach your smallest of children not to do that, and yet he continues to do it. He's very lucky.

"In all seriousness, he hasn't, like, gashed his hand. The FIA obviously needs to have a little look at the podium and do a little sense check on anything that could sparkle its way into the eye of a driver. So there's the first thing that needs a rework."

Lando Norris Brazil victory 'one of his best drives'

Despite his concerns over the celebration, Coulthard was unequivocal in his praise for the drive that preceded it, with Norris managing the switch between intermediate tyres and slicks as rain returned late in the race to threaten his lead.

"It was world-class," Coulthard added. "It was one of his best drives ever. It was awesome because of the nature of that track and the changing conditions, just absolutely phenomenal.

"We're in a wonderful era of Formula 1, where we've got a number of world-class drivers who, given the moment, the car and the confidence, have all got a chance of getting out there and mixing it up."

"Rather worryingly, I guess, for Lando and the other guys, is Max coming from the back to finish second with a car that he was far from happy with, which again is just remarkable."

title: Oscar Piastri issues 'missing the stress' revelation over muted McLaren campaign
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has conceded to 'missing the stress' of fighting for the F1 drivers' championship this season.

Last year, Piastri seemed poised to become Australia's first world champion since the late Alan Jones in 1980, only to suffer a poor final third of the campaign and finish third behind McLaren team-mate Lando Norris and Red Bull's Max Verstappne.

Moving into this season under the new regulations, Piastri has struggled to adapt. He has failed to win a race and only been on the podium twice in 20 races, leaving him a distant seventh in the drivers' standings, 96 points adrift of Norris directly ahead of him.

Asked in an interview with RacingNews365 whether it was a setback not to be involved in the title fight this year, Piastri gave a nuanced answer.

"Yes and no," he said. "I want to be in a championship fight every year if I can be, but also, it's definitely a bit more relaxed this year.

"Obviously, we're not wanting to be in this position, but there's not quite the same stress.

"But that stress that you have in a championship fight is the feeling you want because it means you're fighting for something that is what your goal is.

"I am missing that feeling this year for sure, and it adds a bit of extra intensity and things like that.

"But yeah, it's not all... there are some things that are a little bit easier when you're not in a championship."

[Article continues below]

Piastri - 'Still not easy to drive, even now'

Piastri's drop down the order has coincided with McLaren's difficulties in adapting to the sweeping 2026 technical overhaul, which introduced smaller cars, reduced downforce and a near 50/50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.

McLaren has pointed to customer-team integration issues preventing it from extracting the same performance from its Mercedes power unit as the factory squad, while the team's technical leadership has also flagged sharp downforce losses through medium and high-speed corners as a persistent handicap on the MCL40.

Piastri explained that the scale of the challenge was obvious from the opening races, with the focus initially falling on the power unit rather than the chassis itself.

"It was clear at the beginning of the season that they were going to be quite different, but mainly from the power unit side of things," he said.

"The actual cars themselves are smaller, they have less downforce, so of course they're always going to be different, but I think the first few races we were really occupied with the power unit and how to get the most out of that.

"After the first few races, and especially after they tweaked some of the rules, it became a bit more normal, and that's when we really dug deep into what the car itself is like.

"It wasn't that easy to drive, and it's still not been easy to drive, even now. So, pretty early on we identified that it was going to be challenging.

"It took us a while to understand exactly what needed to change, and then trying to actually change it is tough.

"But we're making progress with it slowly, and that's all we can keep trying to do. So yeah, that's been the biggest thing. We recognised pretty early on that the car had some things that were tricky to manage."

title: Liam Lawson kept waiting as Racing Bulls seat rival handed latest F1 test
excerpt:
Formula 2 title contender Nikola Tsolov will again take to the wheel of F1 machinery this week, RacingNews365 has learned.

Tsolov will take part in a TPC test at the Hungaroring this Wednesday and Thursday, driving an older Honda-powered car.

Budapest is currently experiencing wet and fairly cold conditions, but that is not expected to get in the way of the test going ahead.

Bulgarian Tsolov continues to be linked with a seat at Racing Bulls for next season following his rise through the junior formulae and push for the F2 crown this year.

He goes into the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi trailing Rafael Camara by seven points. Camara made his F1 debut on home soil in Brazil at the weekend with Haas, and will be on the grid permanently with the team next season.

Whilst there has been speculation that Lawson will be retained by Racing Bulls for next season, the wait continues for the team to make an announcement.

Lawson and Arvid Lindblad have formed a strong pairing for the Faenza-based squad this season, delivering the points that leaves the team on the brink of its highest finish in the constructors' championship in its history of fifth.

But whether both drivers will remain at Red Bull's sister team next year is still an open question, with Tsolov very much in the mix. RacingNews365 sources have indicated that no final call has yet been made.

The immediate decision facing Racing Bulls is whether Tsolov or Lawson gets the nod for 2027. But even if the Bulgarian misses out on a permanent F1 seat next year, the plan within Red Bull's driver pool is reportedly to keep him involved regardless.

He is understood to be in line to become Racing Bulls' third driver, with more frequent outings in first practice sessions and TPC tests lined up for him across the season.

title: Mika Häkkinen escapes death after a horrific crash in Australia - On This Day
excerpt:
In 1995, Mika Häkkinen was already being talked about as one of Formula 1's great emerging talents. The Finn finished second twice that season despite driving an unreliable McLaren.

What followed in the years after is well known: Häkkinen developed into Michael Schumacher's fiercest rival, going on to claim back-to-back world titles.

But he came agonisingly close to never getting that chance, after a terrifying accident during Friday qualifying for the 1995 Australian Grand Prix very nearly killed him, 31 years ago today.

Häkkinen was approaching Brewery Bend, a corner on the old Adelaide Street Circuit, at full speed. Unknown to him, his McLaren MP4/10 had a flat tyre. As he braked, the car spun out of control, launched off a curb and went airborne before slamming head-on into a single row of tyre stacks at close to 200 kilometres per hour.

A crash of that magnitude would still be a heavy shunt by modern standards, but rarely a life-threatening one. For comparison, Max Verstappen's impact into the barriers during the 2021 British Grand Prix registered 51G. Häkkinen, however, had no HANS device to protect him, and behind his single row of tyres sat a solid concrete wall.

The consequences were brutal. Without the HANS system, Häkkinen was thrown forward inside the cockpit with such force that his head smashed into the steering wheel, breaking it on impact, before striking the sides of the survival cell.

He suffered a severe skull fracture, internal bleeding, a blocked airway, partial facial paralysis and broken ossicles in his ear.

[Article continues below]

'I realised this was serious'

Häkkinen later gave a detailed account of the crash on the Beyond the Grid podcast, recalling the incident in striking detail.

"I didn't see the guardrail coming because the car was spinning through the air. So when I hit the guardrail, it happened very suddenly. It came as a surprise," Häkkinen said.

"At that moment, my head moved with tremendous force, causing me to fracture my skull. The impact itself was accompanied by a tremendous noise. I still remember sitting in the car and not being able to lift my arms. I couldn't move my legs. I realised this was serious.

"I realised what had happened and told myself, 'Mika, just don't do anything.' Well, I couldn't move anyway. But for some reason, my brain was telling me not to move. Stay calm and wait for help to arrive.

"Fortunately, there was an entire medical team standing by at that specific turn, including doctors. Within 15 to 20 seconds, they were there to help me. That's when they discovered I couldn't breathe."

Two volunteer doctors who happened to be stationed near the crash site rushed to Häkkinen's aid and performed an emergency tracheotomy to clear his blocked airway.

"I remember the pain, and then I lost consciousness," Häkkinen recalled. "I was conscious right up until the moment they cut an opening in my throat."

Häkkinen's condition then deteriorated rapidly. F1's medical delegate at the time, Sid Watkins, had to perform CPR on him twice after arriving at the scene.

Following extensive treatment trackside, Häkkinen was transferred to the Royal Adelaide Hospital, where he was placed in intensive care and treated by neurosurgeons.

He remained in a coma for more than a day before regaining consciousness, and spent around two and a half months in hospital recovering from his injuries.

The story has a happy ending. Häkkinen was back behind the wheel in full force by the start of the 1996 season, and went on to be crowned F1 champion in both 1998 and 1999.

title: F1 branded a ‘smelly old dinosaur’ by Formula E billionaire: ‘It should be a museum'
excerpt:
An Australian billionaire who has entered the world of Formula E had some sharp words to say about Formula 1!

Fortescue founder Dr. Andrew Forrest has launched an extraordinary attack on Formula 1, branding the championship a "smelly old dinosaur", that "it should be a museum" and calling for a head-to-head race against Formula E machinery.

The Australian mining billionaire made the comments at the launch of Fortescue Zero Racing's Gen4 livery, the team he has built after his green energy firm acquired Penske Autosport in September.

Fortescue Zero enters Formula E's 2027 season as the series' first Australian-licensed outfit, running customer Jaguar Gen4 powertrains from its Kidlington base under team principal Jim Wright.

The new outfit traces its roots back to Fortescue's 2022 acquisition of Williams Advanced Engineering, and the group has previously worked within Formula E as the championship's official Pit Boost charging provider as well as a technical partner to Jaguar.

That background in battery and powertrain technology appears to have fuelled Forrest's confidence that his new venture can close the gap on Formula 1 far quicker than many would expect.

Speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, Forrest set out his ambitions for the new team in typically combative fashion.

"The other race which we're going to win is this dream I have," said Forrest.

"I want to see that old dinosaur: noisy, smoky, smelly. Oh, sounds like the fossil fuel sector. No, it's Formula 1!

"I want to see Formula 1 go head-to-head with Formula E, and then I want to say: how many decades did they have to get this right, and how many months did we have to get it right? And let's see how we go."

Formula 1 issued 'time is ticking fast' warning

Asked directly whether F1 still has a place in motorsport, Forrest did not hold back.

Forrest replied: "No, I think Formula 1 has a place. It should have a very large building with Formula 1 on the front of it, made out of limestone, with lights on it, and it should be a museum because the younger generation are going to go to the highest-performance, greatest, technically advanced and kindest-to-the-environment racing there is, and that's going to be Formula E.

"Now, Formula 1 is fantastic, but the time is ticking fast."

Pressed on how such a contest might actually be staged, Forrest pointed to the car unveiled behind him.

"Ah, well, look, you do a head-to-head," he said. "You can take a car like this [the Gen4]. Anyway, it's not up to me, but I'd like to see a car like this go head-to-head with any Formula 1 car in the world, and just see how we go, baby.

"Let's just put it to the test. And I don't care if we come first or second. What I know is that we're doing in months and years what they've taken decades to do. And if we come anywhere near, it's over."

title: Esteban Ocon shares 'heartfelt' statement as F1 career hangs in balance
excerpt:
Esteban Ocon has issued a "heartfelt thank you" to fans who contacted him following his abrupt sacking by Haas, with the Frenchman's F1 future increasingly uncertain.

The 30-year-old was already scheduled to leave the American team at the end of the 2026 season but was dropped early following a dispute with team principal Ayao Komatsu.

In a statement shared on social media, Ocon wrote: "I wanted to say a heartfelt thank you for all your messages. Your support means a great deal to me.

"To the fans, colleagues and former colleagues who have taken the time to reach out as well, I’m truly grateful."

He added: "My love for this sport remains as strong as ever, and I’m grateful to share that passion with so many of you."

Relations had become strained amid Ocon's struggles to match team-mate Oliver Bearman, with Komatsu previously admitting Haas had expected more from the experienced driver.

Tensions escalated at the Mexico City Grand Prix after Ocon argued with race engineer Laura Mueller over tyre selection during practice.

The Frenchman subsequently acknowledged a "difference in viewpoints" with team personnel but strongly denied reports that any confrontation had become physical.

Haas replaced him with Ryo Hirakawa for the Mexican race before confirming he would not return this season. Komatsu insisted the decision was in the team's "best interest", declining to discuss private conversations.

Ferrari academy driver Rafael Câmara, already signed for 2027, subsequently made his F1 debut alongside Bearman in São Paulo.

Ocon made his F1 debut with Manor in 2016 and later raced for Force India, Renault and Alpine, claiming his maiden victory at the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix.

However, with no seat confirmed for 2027, his future in the sport remains in serious doubt.

title: Star-studded documentary to celebrate decade of Formula 2
excerpt:
Formula 2 is marking its 10th season with a new documentary featuring nine current Formula 1 drivers, team principals and senior figures from across the sport.

Titled 'Where F1 Stars are made', the behind-the-scenes film is set to be released on Wednesday 11 November at 14:00 GMT, examining the role of F2 as the final stepping stone before reaching F1.

Filmed throughout the 2026 campaign, it explores the rivalries, pressures and technical challenges facing young drivers, alongside the demands of an F2 race weekend.

Since the modern championship was introduced in 2017, 22 drivers have progressed to F1, with 12 competing on the 2026 grid.

Current F2 championship leader Rafael Câmara added his name to that list at last week's São Paulo Grand Prix.

In the documentary, Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc discusses the pressure of competing in a category "where everyone is looking at you, and you need to prove you can get the F1 seat".

2026 F1 world champion Kimi Antonelli reflects on the importance of being "on the pace straight away", whilst 2025 title winner Lando Norris recalls his battles with future grand prix drivers Alex Albon and George Russell.

F1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali outlines the championship's wider importance to the sport.

"The experience we are giving the drivers, the engineers, the mechanics is beneficial to the ecosystem. The objective is to make sure that everyone who arrives in F1 has to pass through the pyramid of F3 and F2," he said.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff highlights the development opportunities provided by mastering "a powerful car, much more aero and higher engineering skills".

F2 and F3 CEO Bruno Michel also discusses the series' on-track innovations and how it "prepares drivers for the next step".

Further contributions come from Ferrari team principal Frédéric Vasseur and Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies, who assess the significance of the series as its anniversary season approaches its conclusion.

The documentary also examines the dedication and perseverance demanded of drivers seeking to graduate to the top level, and how the championship develops the skills necessary to succeed in F1.

title: F1 confirm final Imola decision as Middle East crisis addressed
excerpt:
The long wait is over and now we finally have our answer - F1 is heading to the troubled Middle East for the final two grands prix.

F1 has told Imola it will not be required as a contingency venue for the end of this season, with the Qatar and Abu Dhabi rounds to go ahead as planned.

The Italian venue had been held in reserve in case F1 decided against finishing the campaign in the Middle East, with any replacement event pencilled in for the Abu Dhabi weekend slot on December 4-6.

That scenario has now been ruled out. Both Imola and the teams have been informed of the decision.

The Emilia-Romagna circuit had always been a fallback option rather than part of the plan to guarantee a 22-race season and meet commercial broadcast commitments should the Gulf double-header be abandoned.

With F1 unable to keep Imola waiting indefinitely, Formula One Management set a deadline of November 10 to stand down the Italian contingency and commit freight logistics to finishing the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

F1 has made clear that nothing has changed on the ground in Qatar or Abu Dhabi to force a rethink, with MotoGP's event in Qatar this past weekend cited as evidence that racing in the region remains viable.

That is despite safety concerns around the Lusail event intensifying after the factory Yamaha MotoGP team withdrew from that race citing corporate travel warnings.

[Article continues below]

Grand Prix

Qatar GP

Door not fully closed on a late change

The wider questions over the region had been triggered by regional tensions involving the United States and Iran, along with threats to maritime and airspace security in the Gulf, which prompted safety evaluations for staging races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

According to the information shared, nothing has negatively developed in the region, and specifically in those two countries, in recent months.

Travel advice still permits travel, travel insurance remains valid, events are continuing to take place, and business has returned to a normal level, with the teams understood to be supportive of concluding the season as planned.

F1 has expressed gratitude for the support and collaboration of the promoter and government in Imola and the region throughout the standby period, during which F1 had funded preliminary temporary grandstand assembly at the circuit so it could rapidly scale spectator capacity on short notice if needed.

The door has not been fully closed on a late change, however, should circumstances shift before the season concludes with the Qatar and Abu Dhabi rounds.

Should the situation develop negatively in the coming weeks before the Middle Eastern events, F1 has indicated it will not hesitate to act accordingly, with the safety of everyone remaining the priority.

title: Fernando Alonso pinpoints 'phenomenal' Aston Martin strength after rare F1 duels
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso believes the performance of his Aston Martin chassis in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix was "phenomenal" as it allowed him to fight with Ferrari and Mercedes cars.

Alonso was able to secure Aston Martin's best grid position of the season in the dreadfully wet qualifying session at Interlagos, lining up in eighth place, and looked set to challenge for much-needed points for the team, which has endured a tricky season.

However, Alonso eventually took the flag in 12th place, outside of the points, with the two Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, the McLaren of Oscar Piastri, and the Red Bull of Max Verstappen all passing him during the 71-lap race, which was run on intermediate tyres at the start and end before around 50 laps on dry, slick tyres.

The Achilles' Heel of the Aston Martin package has been the Honda engine, which is struggling for not only pure power, but also drivability - something key to extracting a good result in wet conditions.

During the spells of the race on the intermediate tyres, Alonso duelled with old rival Hamilton, passing him around the outside on pure pace as the Ferrari sank back down the order after its lightning-fast start.

Reflecting, Alonso felt that taking into account the lack of top-end speed, the car's performance at Interlagos was "phenomenal."

"It was better in the rain for sure, better than the dry," Alonso explained to media, including RacingNews365.

"But all in all, I think the pace was quite okay, and it was a good surprise; the car was performing well throughout the race.

"Obviously, we're still missing a lot of straight-line speed, and that is difficult to compensate for, but at one point, we were in a fight with the Ferraris at the beginning, and even at the end with the Mercedes.

"So taking that into account, we lose a lot on the straights, and that means the car was phenomenal in the corners, so it was a nice feeling.

"It was a better race than weekend; in Free Practice, we were not super happy with the car, but in the race, it hit a better window, so let's see what we can do in the next three."

Alonso was then asked if the performance was simply track- and condition-specific, to which he replied: "There's nothing to learn about the car.

"We are in race 21 now, so we know exactly what we need to improve."

title: Max Verstappen calls for Red Bull investigation: 'There is something wrong'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen is adamant Red Bull must establish what "went wrong" with his car during the São Paulo Grand Prix, after he encountered "extreme" levels of oversteer at Interlagos.

Verstappen scythed through the field in the opening laps, having started down in P21, to finish second behind Lando Norris, in difficult, changeable conditions.

It was yet another imperious performance from the four-time F1 drivers' champion in Brazil. However, whilst the Dutchman was formidable on the intermediate tyres the pack started the 71-lap race on, he was significantly less satisfied with how his RB22 felt after moving onto the two stints on soft tyres in the middle of the grand prix.

Reflecting on the result, Verstappen explained the various problems he was dealing with. Despite the remarkable charge from the back row of the grid to the podium, he was not completely satisfied.

"When you start that far back, you need to try to get by the guys ahead of you as quickly as you can," he told media, including RacingNews365.

"I do think that first stint went really, really well. We got very quickly back into the top 10, and I think the pace wasn't bad.

"But as soon as I switched to the slicks, I had an extreme amount of oversteer in the car in the high-speed corners, which made it super difficult to drive.

"So, we need to understand if something broke on the car, some kind of aero loss or whatever, because this was not normal.

"I sit here, of course, very happy with second, but at the same time, I know there was more in it if the car had been in good shape.

"Unfortunately, that was not the case. I actually did most of the race with a car that was not in good shape, and to finish second, of course, is fantastic."

[Article continues below]

Verstappen hopes for higher Interlagos starting position

Verstappen would be forgiven if he felt he had a case of déjà vu visiting Interlagos, with history seemingly repeating itself when the 29-year-old visits São Paulo.

For the past three years, the Red Bull driver has reached the podium having started well down the order. In 2024, he won from P17 on the grid, and went from the pit lane to third 12 months ago.

If left Verstappen wondering what would have been possible without the power unit grid penalties he incurred, before being beseiged again with the deteriorating issue he and Laurent Mekies have warned about in recent months, whereby the Red Bull degrades in performance across a race.

"Maybe next year I'd love to start a bit further up front instead of starting from the back or the pit lane, but we'll find out next year," he added.

"It's been good. In the wet, it probably also gives you a few more opportunities to get by cars. You can do some different lines and have more opportunities, so that definitely helped me.

"But we also have to understand why or what went wrong with the car as soon as we went to the slick tyres, because even when I switched back to the Inter tyres at the end, the car was night and day different to my first stint, which shows that there is something wrong."

title: FIA reaffirms commitment to ending F1 season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi
excerpt:
The FIA and its President, Mohammed Ben Sulayem, have reiterated their stance that the F1 season will end as planned in the Middle East.

The campaign-concluding triple header is scheduled to see the paddock head from Las Vegas to Qatar and finally to Abu Dhabi.

However, the instability in the Middle East after the start of the United States-Iran war in March has caused considerable uncertainty across the year.

Whilst it has become clearer in recent weeks that Formula 1 can — and most likely will — finish the calendar as designed, there are contingency plans in place.

Imola is on standby to hold a one-off round in place of the finale in early December if F1 does not deem it ultimately safe to visit Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

MotoGP held a round in the former nation last weekend, which should provide further reassurance that the final two F1 weekends can go ahead.

Although the region remains volatile, there has not been a recent escalation in hostilities between the United States and Iran, which led to strikes across the Gulf earlier in 2026.

That not only affected travel to the season-opening Australian Grand Prix, but also saw the rescheduling and relocating of the Bahrain Grand Prix to Malaysia in October and the outright cancellation of the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix.

But as F1 prepares to head back to the Middle East for the first time since pre-season testing, the FIA has reaffirmed the decision with a statement of support.

"The countdown is on for Qatar and Abu Dhabi," Ben Sulayem wrote on a social media post. "We are fully focused on delivering two exceptional grand prix weekends.

"We are working closely with our partners to ensure everything is in place for our drivers, teams and fans.

"We look forward to welcoming everyone for two thrilling weekends of racing and an unforgettable finish to the Formula 1 season."

title: Red Bull retain shock status as FIA make key 2027 F1 announcement
excerpt:
Red Bull-Ford will enter the 2027 Formula 1 season without additional power unit development allowances after the FIA confirmed that its latest ADUO assessment has resulted in no further upgrades being granted.

The decision leaves Red Bull, which was surprisingly identified as the benchmark for internal combustion engine (ICE) performance earlier this year, without the additional homologation opportunities awarded to rival manufacturers.

The FIA has completed its third Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) review of 2026, covering races 12 to 18, with the findings communicated to all five power unit manufacturers.

Although the governing body confirmed that the performance gaps between the manufacturers had changed, no additional homologations were awarded.

It marks the second consecutive review without any further upgrades being granted, leaving the existing allocations unchanged heading into 2027.

Red Bull-Ford's position as the benchmark came as a shock earlier in the campaign, particularly given Mercedes' dominance under the new regulations and Red Bull's status as a first-year engine manufacturer.

However, the FIA's assessment measures ICE performance rather than the complete hybrid power unit, with Red Bull emerging as the benchmark in the opening assessments.

[Article continues below]

How does ADUO work?

Introduced for 2026, ADUO allows manufacturers whose internal combustion engines fall at least two per cent below the leading ICE to undertake additional development.

Manufacturers between two and four per cent behind qualify for one additional homologation in the current season and another the following year, alongside an increased cost cap and dynamometer testing allowances.

Those at least four per cent behind qualify for two additional homologations in each season.

Following the first review, which concluded after the Canadian Grand Prix, Mercedes was placed in the two-to-four per cent category, earning one additional upgrade for 2026 and another for 2027.

Audi, Ferrari and Honda were all more than four per cent behind, qualifying for two additional homologations in each season.

Red Bull received no additional allowances, while the second review, completed after the Hungarian Grand Prix, also produced no further allocations.

The latest findings therefore leave those original allowances intact for 2027, with Red Bull still without any extra development opportunities under ADUO.

FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis defended the assessment process, saying the governing body was confident in its conclusions.

He also acknowledged that discussions were ongoing with manufacturers and teams over potential refinements to the system.

"The FIA has undertaken extensive analysis as part of the review of ADUO this year. Based on the quality of the data and the robustness of the assessment process, we are confident in our findings and the conclusions reached," he said.

"The first year of implementation has also reinforced our belief that the ADUO concept is the right one for Formula 1. However, it is important that the system continues to evolve to ensure it remains efficient, relevant and fit for purpose. To that end, we have been working closely with the Power Unit Manufacturers and teams to explore refinements to the methodology that will support the continued effectiveness of ADUO in future seasons."

The next ADUO review will cover the opening six rounds of the 2027 season, beginning in Bahrain and concluding in Miami.

title: Toto Wolff sends clear message by raising numerous Mercedes questions
excerpt:
Toto Wolff says the 2027 F1 season has already started, as far as he is concerned, after Mercedes wrapped up the constructors' championship at Interlagos.

Heading into the São Paulo Grand Prix, the German marque needed to outscore Ferrari by just three points to secure a ninth title, and its first since 2021.

With George Russell and Kimi Antonelli coming home fourth and fifth, respectively, and Ferrari settling for eighth and ninth from Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, the Brackley-based team was able to cap off a campaign that never really looked like it would end without the crown.

But despite the dominant start to the year, which saw the team win the opening six grands prix, the competition has caught up.

Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull have all won multiple rounds and whilst Mercedes has doubled its tally to 12, there is a clear disparity when comparing the subsequent 14 events to the unbeaten streak to commence the season.

Heading towards winter, it is something Wolff is acutely aware of, even if the changing levels of competitiveness amongst Mercedes' three rivals aided its title bid.

"Look at the last few races; we haven't won," the team principal told media, including RacingNews365.

"At the beginning of the race, Kimi was just storming away; it looked like this could be ours.

"But the competition has been getting tougher. With Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull, and ourselves, it's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship."

[Article continues below]

Questions Wolff wants answers to

Anticipating a tricky title defence, Wolff's stance is that the final three rounds of the year are all in preparation for that challenge.

It has left the Mercedes boss with multiple questions he wants answers to.

"I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year. So for me, the 2027 season has started now," he added.

"It is about learning in the last three races. What is it we can optimise? What didn't we spot when we put the upgrade on the car?

"What is it we can learn to attack these last three races full blast, whilst also making sure that we have the learning for next year's power unit and next year's car?"
